name: Refugees International (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. Haitians paroled into the US (about a third, counted as Haiti's), Sudan's humanitarian response and access from Chad (about 37%), asylum seekers' work permits in Costa Rica (under 5%); the other campaigns (about 30%) over Ukraine, Gaza, the US and Uganda by the annual report's emphasis (a judgment).
summary: Refugees International, a Washington advocacy group that takes no government money, spent $4.5m on advocacy and strategic outreach in 2024 (its latest full audited year). No outcome is measured, so each of its main 2024 results is built from public data and ranged judgments and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: the roughly 97,000 Haitians paroled into the US that year under pathways it pressed for, valued by their gain in consumption and safety for the years they stay; Sudan's $1.9bn 2024 humanitarian response, of which advocacy is credited with a small share, net of the aid it displaced, plus access and diplomacy; and Costa Rica's June 2024 reform giving asylum seekers work permits, from a study of regularisation in Colombia; other campaigns add 40%. It comes to about 0.11 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.01-0.9), about the site's global-health median, between charityevals' estimates for MSF's and Save the Children's advocacy, roughly half from Sudan and half from Haiti. The result is mostly uncertainty: the biggest questions are how much of each result advocacy caused, Refugees International's share of the advocacy, and how long the parolees stay.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Refugees International, advocacy and strategic outreach (2024)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

source.title: US Customs and Border Protection, CBP releases October 2024 monthly update
source.quote: 110,240 Cubans, 211,010 Haitians, 93,070 Nicaraguans, and 117,310 Venezuelans arrived and were granted parole.

rows.explainer: The same cumulative count nine months later.

rows.label: Months between the two counts

source.title: US Customs and Border Protection, monthly updates of January and October 2024

rows.explainer: February to October 2024.

rows.label: Haiti: Haitians paroled into the US in 2024
rows.explainer: The nine months' arrivals scaled to a year: about 97,000, close to Refugees International's own 'over 100,000 Haitians' for 2024 (financial statements, note 1, p. 8). The processes were briefly paused in July-August 2024 for vetting checks, which the scaling averages in. These are the people Refugees International's advocacy for the Haitian parole and family-reunification pathways is credited with helping, below.

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption per person in the US, relative to the lowest-income fifth of US households
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 (0.6-1.4): newly arrived parolees had work authorisation and a US sponsor, mostly in low-wage jobs, so they consume about as the lowest-income fifth of US households does; lower in the first months and for large families, higher for those with family support.

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption per person in the US (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The Consumer Expenditure Survey's spending per person (the site's US baseline, docs/normalization.md 2.14) times the lowest fifth's share, about $14,600, times the judgment above.

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption at home relative to the average Haitian
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-3): the process needed a passport, a flight and a US sponsor with means, so parolees came from better-off households than the average Haitian; 1 if they were typical, 3 if mostly urban middle class.

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption per person had they stayed (US$ a year at US prices)
rows.explainer: Haiti's national-accounts consumption per person (2024) on the survey scale (the site's median survey-to-national-accounts ratio: Haiti has no recent survey), at US prices (the private-consumption PPP factor), times the judgment above: about $4,200.

rows.label: Haiti: gain in log consumption per person-year in the US
rows.explainer: ln(consumption in the US ÷ consumption at home), on the site's one log-income scale, as cash-income does.

rows.label: Haiti: people killed in gang violence, 2024

source.title: UN News, More than 5,600 killed in Haiti gang violence in 2024 (7 January 2025)
source.quote: At least 5,601 people were killed in gang violence in Haiti last year

rows.explainer: The UN human rights office's verified count for 2024.

rows.label: Haiti: share of the risk of a violent death removed by living in the US
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (70-100%): US homicide rates are about a tenth of Haiti's 2024 gang-violence death rate for these mostly urban young adults.

rows.label: Haiti: violent deaths averted per person-year in the US
rows.explainer: Haiti's 2024 gang-violence death rate (deaths over population, about 1 in 2,100 a year) times the share removed.

rows.label: Haiti: share of parolees who wouldn't otherwise have reached the US
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-90%): without the lawful pathway some would have crossed irregularly (Haitians were among the largest groups at the southern border in 2021-2022) and some would have gone to other countries (Chile, Brazil, the Dominican Republic) with smaller gains; most had no other way to leave.

rows.label: Haiti: value per parolee per year in the US (units of value)
rows.explainer: The log-consumption gain plus the violent deaths averted, each death valued at the shared moral weight for ages 15-49 (most parolees are working-age adults; children came with them) times the value-of-life slider, for the share who wouldn't otherwise have come.

rows.label: Haiti: years a parolee stays in the US
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 (1.5-15): parole was for two years, and the processes were ended in 2025 (DHS terminated CHNV in March 2025); many applied for asylum or Temporary Protected Status, or stayed without status, and few were removed to Haiti while its airports and capital were under gang control. 1.5 if most leave or are removed when parole ends, 15 if most settle.

rows.label: Haiti: years in the US, discounted
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate. A parolee's years are their own, not a won reform's (rights-advocacy: a released person's years), so not $win_years_counted.

rows.label: Haiti: value to family at home through remittances, as a share of the parolee's own gain
rows.explainer: A side effect: parolees send money to relatives in Haiti, where a dollar goes much further on the log scale. Judgment 20% (5-50%): remittances are about a fifth of Haiti's national income and the parolees' own consumption above is net of what they send.

rows.label: Haiti: loss to Haiti from the departure of skilled people, as a share of the parolees' gain
rows.explainer: A side effect: nurses, teachers and other skilled workers were among those who left. Judgment -5% (-15% to -1%): the parolees are a small share of Haiti's workforce (about 1%), and remittances (above) offset part of it.

rows.label: Haiti: value of 2024's parolees (units of value)
rows.explainer: Parolees × value per person-year × discounted years, plus the side effects. A year's arrivals against a year's spending (the pathways had to be defended each year: a Texas-led lawsuit against them was dismissed in March 2024).

rows.label: Sudan: humanitarian funding to the 2024 response plan (US$)

source.title: OCHA Financial Tracking Service, Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2024 (plan 1188)
source.note: Read from the FTS public API, https://api.hpc.tools/v1/public/fts/flow?planId=1188&groupby=plan

rows.explainer: Funding reported to OCHA's Financial Tracking Service against Sudan's 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan ($2.70bn required, about 70% funded; 2023's plan was about 43% funded). Refugees International's 'Speak Out on Sudan' campaign with diaspora groups pressed for aid, access and diplomacy throughout 2024.

rows.label: Sudan: value of a dollar of the humanitarian response, as a multiple of cash
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5× (0.2-1.5×): charityevals' estimates of humanitarian responses come to about a fifth to two fifths of cash per dollar after their own adjustments (Save the Children's emergencies, MSF's relief distributions); charityevals' MSF advocacy model values appeal funding at 1×. Sudan's 2024 response was food, water, health care and cash in a declared famine with very high death rates, so above the average response; agencies' overheads and access problems pull it down.

rows.label: Sudan: value of a dollar of the response (units of value)
rows.explainer: The multiple × the site's value of a dollar given as cash (@cash.uov_per_dollar).

rows.label: Sudan: share of the extra funding taken from other aid
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (20-80%): donors' humanitarian budgets are mostly set, so money that advocacy steers to Sudan partly comes from other crises; some is new (supplementary appropriations, pledging conferences such as Paris in April 2024).

rows.label: Sudan: value of the other aid displaced, per dollar (units of value)
rows.explainer: A side effect: the displaced aid's value, lost, at the same multiple of cash (other crises' responses are of the same kind).

rows.label: Sudan: access and diplomacy, as a share of the funding effect
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (0-200%): besides funding, the campaign pressed for aid access (the Adre crossing from Chad, reopened in August 2024), the US special envoy (appointed February 2024), the US determination of atrocities and genocide, and pressure on the UAE over arms to the RSF. None has a measured effect; 0 if they changed nothing on the ground, 200% if reopened crossings did more than the money.

rows.label: Sudan: years until the funding is spent
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5 (0.25-1): funding to a response plan is spent within the year or soon after.

rows.label: Sudan: discount for the wait
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Sudan: value of the 2024 response funding (units of value)
rows.explainer: Funding × the value of a dollar net of the aid it displaces, plus access and diplomacy, discounted for the wait. A year's funding against a year's spending; the share advocacy added and Refugees International's part are below.

rows.label: Costa Rica: work permits issued a year to asylum seekers under the 2024 rules

source.title: UNHCR, Costa Rica Annual Results Report 2024
source.quote: enabling the issuance of 20,000 work permits and the renewal of 22,000
source.note: UNHCR's site returns 403 to automated fetches; the sentence as shown in search results on 2026-11-14.

rows.explainer: UNHCR credits Executive Decree 44501-MGP (12 June 2024), which partly reversed the 2022 decree 43810-MGP that had removed asylum seekers' immediate work permits, with 20,000 work permits issued (and 22,000 renewed) in 2024. Taken as a year's flow: the first months cleared a backlog, and about 2,100 new asylum claims arrive each month (UNHCR, 2024), about 25,000 a year who need permits. The publisher blocks automated downloads; figure from its 2024 Annual Results Report as indexed.

rows.label: Costa Rica: share of those permits that the 2022 rules would have blocked
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (15-70%): under the 2022 decree an asylum seeker could get a permit only after three months and with social-security (CCSS) enrolment, which needs a formal employer, and not for self-employment; the 2024 rules put the permit on the asylum seeker's identity card. Many would still have got a permit, later.

rows.label: Costa Rica: people sharing the gain of one permit
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-2.5): the gain is in household consumption per person, shared with children and partners; many households have more than one permit holder.

rows.label: Costa Rica: people a year gaining from the right to work
rows.explainer: Permits a year × the share the reform made possible × the people sharing each.

rows.label: Costa Rica: consumption gain from regularisation for forced migrants (Colombia's PEP)

source.title: Ibáñez, Moya, Ortega, Rozo and Urbina, Life out of the Shadows: Impacts of Amnesties in the Lives of Refugees (IZA DP 15049, 2022; JEEA 2025)
source.quote: consumption per capita (a gain of 48%), monthly labor income (an increase of 22%)
source.note: The published abstract (Journal of the European Economic Association 23(3), 2025, pp. 941-982); the 2022 working paper (https://docs.iza.org/dp15049.pdf) reports 60 percent.

rows.explainer: Ibáñez et al. (Life out of the Shadows, IZA DP 15049; Journal of the European Economic Association 2025), a natural experiment on Venezuelan migrants in Colombia: regularisation under the PEP raised consumption per person by 60% in the working paper and 48% in the published version. Best guess the published figure; range from 30% to the working paper's 60%.

rows.label: Costa Rica: share of the regularisation effect that a work permit alone brings
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (15-70%): the PEP gave legal status, work rights, health insurance and bank accounts; asylum seekers in Costa Rica already had legal stay, and the 2024 change adds a work permit from the start and self-employment. The paper attributes much of the gain to access to services, not only work.

rows.label: Costa Rica: value per person per year (units of value)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + the consumption gain a work permit brings) × the site's value of a doubling of consumption.

rows.label: Costa Rica: chance the change happens
rows.explainer: The decree was issued in June 2024 and applied from July, so 1; how much was advocates' doing is the counterfactual below.

rows.label: Costa Rica: years the change counts
rows.explainer: A won reform counts the site's shared years brought forward ($win_years_counted, docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Costa Rica: years until the change takes effect
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.1 (0-0.3): published in June 2024, permits on the new cards from July.

rows.label: Costa Rica: discount for the wait
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Costa Rica: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: The years counted, discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Costa Rica: value of the reform (units of value)
rows.explainer: People a year × value per person-year × the chance × the discounted years counted.

rows.label: Costa Rica: years of campaigning behind the win
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-2.5): Refugees International and IRCA Casabierta, a refugee-led organisation, contested the November 2022 decrees from their issue (joint statement, December 2022) until the June 2024 reform.

rows.label: Costa Rica: value per year of campaigning, at 2024's budget (units of value)
rows.explainer: The win over the years of spending behind it, scaled to 2024's budget, so it sets against the 2024 cost.

rows.label: Other campaigns' results, as a share of the three modelled
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (10-150%): the 2024 annual report names other work with no measured result: localisation of aid in Ukraine (two reports it says led to more aid from state donors directly to Ukrainian organisations), the Gaza scorecard with seven other agencies on aid obstruction, LGBTQ+ refugees' access to jobs in Costa Rica, the Destination Reception Assistance Act it helped draft and the #LetAsylumSeekersWork bill (neither passed), climate displacement at COP29 and in Uganda's adaptation plan, the Refugee Fellows, and the Refugee Advocacy Lab's public support for US resettlement (about 500 state and local officials' letter). Anchor: about nine campaigns, three modelled; if the others are worth a twelfth of a modelled win each, 40%; 10% if they mostly changed words, 150% if Ukraine's localisation moved large sums.

rows.label: Haiti parole: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.8 (0.5-1): the gain is a cross-country consumption gap, not measured for these parolees; studies of migrants' earnings at the same skill (the 'place premium') find gains as large or larger, but parolees' first years are below their later earnings.

rows.label: Haiti parole: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (3-30%): the processes were the administration's own border policy, launched in January 2023 alongside expulsions at the border; advocates pressed for Haitians' inclusion, family reunification and keeping the pathway open. 3% if it would have run the same without them, 30% if advocacy kept it going against the 2024 lawsuit and political pressure.

rows.label: Haiti parole: Refugees International's share of the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 5% (2-15%): many groups pressed for the Haitian pathways (Haitian Bridge Alliance, Welcome.US, the resettlement agencies, IRAP, HIAS, the Haitian diaspora, members of Congress); Refugees International names its part in its 2024 accounts, as one of several Washington voices.

rows.label: Haiti parole: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: the arrivals are counted, but the advocacy's part and the parolees' gains are judgments, not measured. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Haiti parole: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Sudan: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.7 (0.4-1): the value of a dollar of the response is a judgment, not measured for Sudan's 2024 plan.

rows.label: Sudan: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (1-8%) of 2024's Sudan funding added by advocacy as a whole: funding rose from 43% of the plan in 2023 to about 70% in 2024, mostly from the famine and the scale of the war; advocates moved the margin, as for charityevals' Save the Children Gavi branch (3%). 1% if donors would have given the same, 8% if the campaign held up the US's and other large donors' pledges.

rows.label: Sudan: Refugees International's share of the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 5% (2-12%): Refugees International was one of the main US voices on Sudan in 2024 (its President testified and led the 'Speak Out on Sudan' campaign with diaspora groups), beside the IRC, NRC, MSF, Oxfam, Save the Children, Mercy Corps, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and the UN agencies themselves.

rows.label: Sudan: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured effect of the campaign on funding or access. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Sudan: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Costa Rica: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.6 (0.3-1): the effect is from a Colombian regularisation that gave more than a work permit, applied to a narrower change in another country.

rows.label: Costa Rica: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (5-50%): the share of the reform due to advocates at all. The Constitutional Court had already struck down another part of the 2022 decree, UNHCR pressed the government, and the backlog made the old rules costly to run; advocates' pressure moved the timing and content.

rows.label: Costa Rica: Refugees International's share of the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (5-35%): Refugees International's share with IRCA Casabierta (its partner, whose work its grants support), among UNHCR, other NGOs and litigants.

rows.label: Costa Rica: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: the permits are counted by UNHCR, but the effect is from another country's programme and the advocacy's part is a judgment. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Costa Rica: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj * hai_evidence_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj * sdn_evidence_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj * cri_evidence_adj) / (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Counterfactual (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj * hai_counterfactual_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj * sdn_counterfactual_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj * cri_counterfactual_adj) / (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of the resources behind the outcome (outcome-weighted average, for reading only)
rows.formula: (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj * hai_attribution_share + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj * sdn_attribution_share + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj * cri_attribution_share) / (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own share.

rows.label: Missing-data discount (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj * hai_missing_data_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj * sdn_missing_data_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj * cri_missing_data_adj) / (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj * hai_total_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj * sdn_total_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj * cri_total_adj) / (hai_value_per_year * hai_total_adj + sdn_value_per_year * sdn_total_adj + cri_value_per_year * cri_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities (US$)
rows.explainer: Refugees International doesn't raise money for other charities; its grants to partners ($212,000) are in its own advocacy spending, and the humanitarian funding its campaigns helped win is valued above as won policy (its destination is UN-coordinated response plans, not the site's moved-money destinations).

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of the charity's cost
rows.explainer: Context, and the donors' share of the resources with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention, Helen Keller Intl's vitamin A, New Incentives), each at its result on this site under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Unused here (no money moved): the template's destination, GiveWell's Top Charities, live.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
Careers changed
rows.explainer: Refugees International doesn't move people into other organisations' jobs as a programme (its Refugee Fellows are refugee leaders it trains for their own advocacy, counted in the other campaigns above), so this branch is 0.

rows.label: Pay a career changer gives up per year (US$)
rows.explainer: Unused here (no careers changed); the template's placeholder range.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays in high-impact work
rows.explainer: Unused here (no careers changed); the template's placeholder range.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays, discounted
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of the new employers' work (units of value)
rows.explainer: Unused here (no careers changed): the template's value of a career's employer, a dollar moved.
